# FDE Exam Topic Taxonomy (weighted)

<!-- Generated by tools/taxonomy.py from data/taxonomy.yaml (v1, 2026-10-20). Edit the YAML, not this file. -->

Forward Deployed Engineer examination, role-agnostic. The Gorilla Logic Senior FDE (AI Platform) job description is used as a coverage floor (every non-generic item must map to at least one subtopic), not as a bias.

Weights are the approximate share of a full examination. They come from four kinds of evidence: the job description's coverage requirements, the syllabi of existing FDE and adjacent certifications, how much each handbook covers the topic, and which CandiTech question formats can assess it. The reasoning is in [research.md](research.md); each domain's rationale is below.

## Domains at a glance

| # | Domain | Weight | MCQs in a 220-item bank | Subtopics |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| D1 | FDE Role, Operating Model & Economics | 6% | 13 | 4 |
| D2 | Discovery, Scoping & Delivery Lifecycle | 10% | 22 | 5 |
| D3 | Stakeholders, Communication & Adoption | 9% | 20 | 4 |
| D4 | LLM Application Engineering | 12% | 26 | 5 |
| D5 | Retrieval, RAG & Enterprise Data | 11% | 24 | 5 |
| D6 | Agents, Orchestration & Hybrid Systems | 13% | 29 | 5 |
| D7 | Evaluation & Quality | 10% | 22 | 5 |
| D8 | Governance, Security & Responsible AI | 9% | 20 | 5 |
| D9 | Integration & Distributed Systems | 8% | 18 | 4 |
| D10 | Cloud Deployment & Platform | 5% | 11 | 3 |
| D11 | Observability, Reliability & Cost | 7% | 15 | 4 |
| | **Total** | **100%** | **220** | **49** |

Grouped differently:

- **Field craft: role, discovery, stakeholders**: 25%
- **AI engineering: LLM, RAG/data, agents, evals**: 46%
- **Enterprise production: governance, integration, deployment, operations**: 29%

## Domains and subtopics

`Tag` is the identifier used to tag questions. `Eff.` is the effective weight in the whole exam (domain weight × subtopic share). `MCQs` is the target count in the bank.

### D1 · FDE Role, Operating Model & Economics — 6%

*Why this weight:* Both handbooks spend most pages here (Richard Xu Parts 1, 5, 6), but a skills test samples it lightly: certifications fold it into one "mindset" module (GSDC 1 of 13) and the Adaface FDE test has none. Kept small and principle-only because this is where book-specific theory is densest.

*Sources:* Richard Xu ch01, ch02, ch03, ch04, ch05, ch19, ch20, ch21, ch22, ch26; goday ch1; external: [palantir-dev-delta](https://blog.palantir.com/dev-versus-delta-demystifying-engineering-roles-at-palantir-ad44c2a6e87), [yc-mcgrew-fde](https://podcast.app/the-fde-playbook-for-ai-startups-with-bob-mcgrew-e425046129), [gsdc-cfde](https://www.gsdcouncil.org/certified-forward-deployed-engineer)

| ID | Tag | Subtopic | Share | Eff. | MCQs | Key concepts |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| D1.1 | `role.definition` | What an FDE is accountable for | 30% | 1.8% | 4 | • Outcome accountability in the customer's real environment, not feature delivery<br>• "One customer, many capabilities" (Delta) vs "one capability, many customers" (Dev) — Palantir<br>• Echo (deployment strategist / problem owner) vs Delta (builder) split<br>• Why AI labs revived the role (deployment gap between model capability and enterprise value) |
| D1.2 | `role.adjacent` | FDE vs adjacent roles | 20% | 1.2% | 3 | • Solutions engineer / presales, solutions architect, consultant / SI, customer success, professional services<br>• Discriminators — who writes production code, where it lives, who owns the outcome, how work is priced |
| D1.3 | `role.productization` | Field-to-product feedback and productization | 30% | 1.8% | 4 | • Core platform vs customer-specific code; configuration over customization; no per-customer forks<br>• When to generalize a repeated customization (rule of three) and who decides<br>• Reusable field assets — connectors, templates, eval sets, failure-mode libraries<br>• Per-customer customization effort should fall over time or it is a services business |
| D1.4 | `role.economics` | Engagement economics | 20% | 1.2% | 2 | • Services vs software margins; why FDE-heavy models are a deliberate trade<br>• Pricing models (time & materials, fixed scope, outcome-based) and who carries which risk<br>• ROI against the real baseline (cost of the human process replaced), TCO, build / buy / partner |

### D2 · Discovery, Scoping & Delivery Lifecycle — 10%

*Why this weight:* The defining FDE skill per Palantir's decomposition interview, every certification syllabus and both handbooks; also an explicit JD duty ("discovery in unfamiliar client environments, then fast progress to production"). Best tested by scenarios and open text.

*Sources:* Richard Xu ch06, ch07, ch08, ch09, appA; goday ch1, ch2, ch3; external: [palantir-decomposition](https://www.tryexponent.com/guides/palantir-forward-deployed-engineer-interview), [gsdc-cfde](https://www.gsdcouncil.org/certified-forward-deployed-engineer), [aiu-cfde](https://aiu.ac/training/cfde/)

| ID | Tag | Subtopic | Share | Eff. | MCQs | Key concepts |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| D2.1 | `discovery.framing` | Problem framing and decomposition | 25% | 2.5% | 6 | • Stated request vs underlying problem; observe the workflow, don't only interview<br>• Issue trees / MECE decomposition of a vague problem<br>• End user vs buyer vs sponsor needs |
| D2.2 | `discovery.selection` | Choosing the problem worth solving | 20% | 2.0% | 5 | • Value x feasibility x data availability x risk x sponsorship<br>• When AI is the wrong tool (deterministic rule, report or form will do)<br>• Measurable baseline exists before you start |
| D2.3 | `discovery.environment` | Working in an unfamiliar client environment | 15% | 1.5% | 3 | • System archaeology — undocumented schemas, legacy code, tribal knowledge<br>• Data and access inventory before design; who grants access and how long it takes<br>• Prototyping against real data early |
| D2.4 | `delivery.scoping` | Scoping PoC, pilot, MVP and production | 20% | 2.0% | 4 | • PoC vs pilot vs MVP vs production; a pilot needs real users, real data, real workflow<br>• Success metrics and acceptance criteria agreed before building<br>• Time-boxing, cutting scope not value, managing scope creep; first version is disposable |
| D2.5 | `delivery.go-live` | Production readiness and rollout | 20% | 2.0% | 4 | • The PoC-to-production gap ("pilot purgatory") and its usual causes<br>• Production readiness review — acceptance criteria, ownership, on-call, runbooks, rollback<br>• Progressive rollout — shadow mode, limited cohort, percentage ramp |

### D3 · Stakeholders, Communication & Adoption — 9%

*Why this weight:* CandiTech emphasises open-text and video answers graded by AI rubrics, and its AI-skills material asks candidates to explain and defend decisions — this domain is where those formats land. JD: "communicate trade-offs to client engineers, architects and leadership".

*Sources:* Richard Xu ch15, ch16, ch17, ch08; goday ch2; external: [canditech-ai-skills](https://www.canditech.io/blog/ai-skill-assessment-ai-skills-test/), [gsdc-cfde](https://www.gsdcouncil.org/certified-forward-deployed-engineer)

| ID | Tag | Subtopic | Share | Eff. | MCQs | Key concepts |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| D3.1 | `comms.tradeoffs` | Communicating trade-offs and uncertainty | 25% | 2.2% | 5 | • Bottom line first (Pyramid Principle / BLUF) for executives; depth for engineers<br>• Design docs and decision records; stating options, costs and risks<br>• Explaining probabilistic AI behaviour and its limits to non-technical stakeholders |
| D3.2 | `comms.stakeholders` | Stakeholder management | 25% | 2.2% | 5 | • Stakeholder mapping — sponsor, buyer, users, IT, security, legal, blockers<br>• Handling pushback and resistant IT / security teams; earning trust through evidence<br>• Expectation management, saying no, escalation paths |
| D3.3 | `adoption.change` | Adoption and change management | 25% | 2.2% | 5 | • Go-live is not adoption; define and measure activation and usage<br>• Embedding in existing workflows; incentives over training; fear of replacement<br>• Executive sponsorship for cross-department change; gradual rollout |
| D3.4 | `adoption.handoff` | Handoff and enablement | 25% | 2.2% | 5 | • Exit criteria; documentation, runbooks and knowledge transfer<br>• Customer can operate, change and troubleshoot without you; avoiding vendor dependency<br>• Support model after handoff |

### D4 · LLM Application Engineering — 12%

*Why this weight:* Core of every AI-era FDE syllabus (GSDC prompt engineering module; CCA-F "Prompt Engineering & Structured Output" 20%; Adaface FDE test 8/16 MCQs on prompting + generative AI) and an explicit JD requirement.

*Sources:* Richard Xu ch14; goday ch8; external: [cca-f](https://rickhigh.substack.com/p/claude-certified-architect-the-complete), [adaface-fde](https://www.adaface.com/assessment-test/forward-deployed-engineer-test), [gsdc-cfde](https://www.gsdcouncil.org/certified-forward-deployed-engineer)

| ID | Tag | Subtopic | Share | Eff. | MCQs | Key concepts |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| D4.1 | `llm.fundamentals` | Model and API fundamentals | 20% | 2.4% | 5 | • Tokens, context windows, sampling (temperature, top-p), non-determinism<br>• Latency (time to first token, output length), streaming, rate limits, batch APIs<br>• Prompt caching and what invalidates it |
| D4.2 | `llm.prompting` | Prompt and context engineering | 20% | 2.4% | 5 | • System prompts, clear instructions, examples (few-shot), delimiters / tags<br>• Reasoning / thinking models and when explicit step-by-step helps<br>• Context budgeting, long-context pitfalls, what to put in vs retrieve |
| D4.3 | `llm.structured-tools` | Structured outputs and tool calling | 25% | 3.0% | 7 | • JSON schema / constrained decoding vs "please return JSON"; validate and repair<br>• Tool calling mechanics — the model proposes, the application executes and returns results<br>• Writing tool definitions the model can use correctly |
| D4.4 | `llm.model-selection` | Model selection and adaptation | 20% | 2.4% | 5 | • Choosing by capability, latency, cost, context length, data residency<br>• Routing and cascades (small model first, escalate on low confidence)<br>• Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning vs tools — which problem each solves<br>• Hosted API vs open-weight self-hosted; abstraction to limit lock-in |
| D4.5 | `llm.failure-modes` | LLM failure modes | 15% | 1.8% | 4 | • Hallucination and its causes; knowledge cutoff<br>• Prompt injection (direct and indirect), jailbreaks<br>• Prompt brittleness across model versions; sycophancy |

### D5 · Retrieval, RAG & Enterprise Data — 11%

*Why this weight:* JD lists "SQL, retrieval, indexing and vector stores" and "enterprise context" as requirements; GSDC has dedicated RAG and data-engineering modules; goday spends three chapters on data. CandiTech's SQL question type makes hands-on SQL likely in any data-touching assessment.

*Sources:* Richard Xu ch10, ch13; goday ch3, ch4, ch7; external: [gsdc-cfde](https://www.gsdcouncil.org/certified-forward-deployed-engineer), [canditech-question-types](https://helpcenter.canditech.io/en/articles/8512793-question-types)

| ID | Tag | Subtopic | Share | Eff. | MCQs | Key concepts |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| D5.1 | `rag.retrieval` | Retrieval mechanics | 30% | 3.3% | 7 | • Embeddings, similarity metrics, chunking strategies and their trade-offs<br>• Vector indexes (ANN / HNSW) and recall vs latency<br>• Hybrid search (BM25 + dense), fusion (reciprocal rank fusion), cross-encoder reranking<br>• Query rewriting / expansion |
| D5.2 | `rag.ingestion` | Ingestion, freshness and permissions | 20% | 2.2% | 5 | • Parsing PDFs and tables; metadata; deduplication<br>• Incremental indexing and freshness<br>• Permission-aware retrieval (filter by the caller's ACLs at query time)<br>• Citations / source attribution in answers |
| D5.3 | `rag.architecture` | Choosing a context strategy | 15% | 1.6% | 4 | • RAG vs long context vs fine-tuning vs live API / tool lookups<br>• Agentic retrieval; structured data belongs in SQL, not in a vector store<br>• Repos, tickets, docs and search as context sources |
| D5.4 | `data.sql` | SQL and data discovery | 25% | 2.8% | 6 | • Joins, aggregation, window functions, CTEs, NULL semantics<br>• Discovering undocumented schemas; profiling and data-quality checks<br>• Indexes and reading a query plan at a basic level<br>• Text-to-SQL risks (read-only roles, row limits, validation) |
| D5.5 | `data.modeling` | Data modeling and pipelines | 10% | 1.1% | 2 | • OLTP vs OLAP; star schema; layered raw / cleaned / curated pipelines<br>• ETL vs ELT; data contracts between producers and consumers |

### D6 · Agents, Orchestration & Hybrid Systems — 13%

*Why this weight:* Largest domain. It is the centre of the JD ("AI Harness", hybrid systems, orchestration, "when to use agents vs deterministic workflows"), the top CCA-F domain (Agentic Architecture 27% + Tool Design & MCP 18%), and a dedicated module in every FDE certification.

*Sources:* Richard Xu ch09, ch11; goday ch8; external: [anthropic-building-effective-agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents), [mcp-spec](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification), [cca-f](https://rickhigh.substack.com/p/claude-certified-architect-the-complete), [gsdc-cfde](https://www.gsdcouncil.org/certified-forward-deployed-engineer)

| ID | Tag | Subtopic | Share | Eff. | MCQs | Key concepts |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| D6.1 | `agents.when` | Agents vs workflows vs automation vs traditional software | 25% | 3.2% | 7 | • Workflow: predefined code path with LLM steps. Agent: the model directs its own steps and tool use<br>• Choose by predictability of the path, cost of error, auditability needs, latency and cost budget<br>• Start with the simplest thing that works; add autonomy only when it pays<br>• Plain software or RPA when inputs are structured and rules are known |
| D6.2 | `agents.patterns` | Composition patterns | 20% | 2.6% | 6 | • Prompt chaining with programmatic gates; routing; parallelization (sectioning, voting)<br>• Orchestrator-workers; evaluator-optimizer<br>• The agent loop (reason, act, observe) and explicit stopping conditions |
| D6.3 | `agents.tools-mcp` | Tools and the Model Context Protocol | 20% | 2.6% | 6 | • Tool design for agents — narrow scope, clear names and descriptions, useful errors, idempotent actions<br>• MCP architecture — host, client, server; tools, resources, prompts; stdio vs HTTP transports<br>• Too many tools degrades selection; agent-to-agent protocols (A2A) at awareness level |
| D6.4 | `agents.state` | State, memory and durable execution | 20% | 2.6% | 6 | • Short-term (context) vs long-term memory; context compaction<br>• Checkpointing and resuming long runs (e.g. after an overnight approval)<br>• Retries, scheduling, idempotency of side-effecting steps |
| D6.5 | `agents.multi` | Multi-agent systems and human steps | 15% | 1.9% | 4 | • Supervisor / hierarchical / handoff topologies<br>• When multi-agent helps (parallel breadth) and when it hurts (coordination cost, compounding errors)<br>• Human approval steps inside automated flows |

### D7 · Evaluation & Quality — 10%

*Why this weight:* Both handbooks treat evaluation as the bridge from demo to production; the JD lists a full eval stack; CCA-F "Context Management & Reliability" 15%. Mainstream practice (golden datasets, regression suites, LLM-as- judge) is consistent across sources, so this is high-signal and low-ambiguity.

*Sources:* Richard Xu ch12, ch13; goday ch9; external: [anthropic-demystifying-evals](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents), [ragas](https://docs.ragas.io/en/stable/concepts/metrics/)

| ID | Tag | Subtopic | Share | Eff. | MCQs | Key concepts |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| D7.1 | `eval.datasets` | Eval datasets | 25% | 2.5% | 6 | • Golden datasets built from real cases and edge cases<br>• Regression suites that grow with every production failure<br>• Versioning; leakage; eval-driven development |
| D7.2 | `eval.methods` | Grading methods | 25% | 2.5% | 6 | • Code-based graders (exact match, schema, unit tests) before model graders<br>• LLM-as-judge with rubrics; pairwise comparison; position, verbosity and self-preference bias<br>• Calibrating judges against human labels |
| D7.3 | `eval.rag-agent` | RAG and agent metrics | 20% | 2.0% | 4 | • Faithfulness / groundedness, answer relevance, context precision and recall<br>• Agent task success vs trajectory / tool-call correctness<br>• pass@k vs pass^k (reliability across repeated trials); cost and latency per task |
| D7.4 | `eval.gates` | Thresholds, gates and comparisons | 15% | 1.5% | 3 | • Release gates in CI; thresholds per metric<br>• Model and prompt comparison; re-running evals on model upgrades<br>• Small-sample noise; when a difference is real |
| D7.5 | `eval.online` | Online evaluation | 15% | 1.5% | 3 | • Offline vs online evaluation; sampling production traffic for review<br>• User feedback signals; drift; hallucination checks in production |

### D8 · Governance, Security & Responsible AI — 9%

*Why this weight:* A full JD bullet (identity, permissions, approval gates, guardrails, audit trails, kill switches) and three Richard Xu chapters. Enterprise AI deployments stall here more than anywhere else, so scenario questions are realistic.

*Sources:* Richard Xu ch10, ch11, ch13; goday ch5, ch6; external: [owasp-llm-top10](https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/), [aiu-cfde](https://aiu.ac/training/cfde/)

| ID | Tag | Subtopic | Share | Eff. | MCQs | Key concepts |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| D8.1 | `gov.identity` | Identity and access for agents | 25% | 2.2% | 5 | • SSO (OIDC / SAML), OAuth 2.0 flows, scopes<br>• Delegated (on-behalf-of the user) vs service identity; an agent should not exceed the user's permissions<br>• Least privilege, RBAC vs ABAC, workload identity instead of long-lived keys, secrets management |
| D8.2 | `gov.guardrails` | Guardrails and injection defence | 25% | 2.2% | 5 | • Input / output filtering; PII redaction<br>• Treat retrieved and tool content as untrusted; privilege separation; tool allowlists<br>• Validate tool parameters before any side effect; sandbox code execution |
| D8.3 | `gov.approvals` | Approval gates and kill switches | 20% | 1.8% | 4 | • Human approval tiered by risk, reversibility and blast radius — not on every action<br>• Approval as a durable, auditable step (not a click-through prompt)<br>• Kill switches, action rate limits, dry-run modes |
| D8.4 | `gov.audit-compliance` | Audit, data protection and compliance | 20% | 1.8% | 4 | • Audit trails — who, what, when, on whose behalf, inputs, outputs, tool calls<br>• Data residency, retention, provider data-use terms<br>• GDPR, HIPAA, SOC 2 at awareness level; data sensitivity drives the deployment model |
| D8.5 | `gov.responsible-ai` | Responsible AI | 10% | 0.9% | 2 | • Bias, transparency, explainability through citations<br>• Risk-tiered regulation (e.g. EU AI Act) at awareness level |

### D9 · Integration & Distributed Systems — 8%

*Why this weight:* JD requirements (APIs, async, events, REST, GraphQL, webhooks, queues) and the Adaface FDE test devotes half its MCQs to backend and system design. Mainstream, well-defined material; good MCQ territory.

*Sources:* Richard Xu ch14; goday ch10; external: [adaface-fde](https://www.adaface.com/assessment-test/forward-deployed-engineer-test), [gsdc-cfde](https://www.gsdcouncil.org/certified-forward-deployed-engineer)

| ID | Tag | Subtopic | Share | Eff. | MCQs | Key concepts |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| D9.1 | `int.apis` | API styles and webhooks | 25% | 2.0% | 5 | • REST semantics, pagination, versioning; GraphQL trade-offs<br>• Webhooks — signature verification, retries, idempotency keys, replay protection |
| D9.2 | `int.async` | Async and event-driven design | 30% | 2.4% | 5 | • Queues and streams; at-least-once delivery and idempotent consumers; ordering; dead-letter queues<br>• Sagas and compensation; backpressure; long-running jobs and status callbacks<br>• Choosing sync vs async |
| D9.3 | `int.resilience` | Resilience patterns | 25% | 2.0% | 4 | • Timeouts, retries with exponential backoff and jitter, circuit breakers<br>• Rate limiting, graceful degradation and fallbacks (including to humans)<br>• Consistency trade-offs, caching |
| D9.4 | `int.enterprise-devex` | Enterprise integrations and developer experience | 20% | 1.6% | 4 | • SaaS integrations (GitHub, Jira, Slack, Azure DevOps) — OAuth apps, rate limits, webhooks<br>• Adapters / anti-corruption layers for legacy systems<br>• SDK, CLI, template and config design; documentation as a product |

### D10 · Cloud Deployment & Platform — 5%

*Why this weight:* JD requires one cloud plus containers, serverless, CI/CD, IaC, IAM. Kept vendor-neutral and principle-level: goday's GCP-specific chapters are vendor detail, and CandiTech generic tests are unlikely to go deep on one cloud.

*Sources:* Richard Xu ch10; goday ch5, ch6, ch10; external: [gsdc-cfde](https://www.gsdcouncil.org/certified-forward-deployed-engineer), [aiu-cfde](https://aiu.ac/training/cfde/)

| ID | Tag | Subtopic | Share | Eff. | MCQs | Key concepts |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| D10.1 | `deploy.compute` | Compute choices | 30% | 1.5% | 3 | • Containers and Kubernetes basics; serverless trade-offs (cold starts, max duration vs long LLM calls)<br>• Picking compute for long-running agent workloads |
| D10.2 | `deploy.delivery` | CI/CD and infrastructure as code | 30% | 1.5% | 3 | • Pipelines, environment parity, IaC (e.g. Terraform) and drift<br>• Canary, blue / green, feature flags, rollback |
| D10.3 | `deploy.models-network` | Deployment models and network security | 40% | 2.0% | 5 | • Multi-tenant SaaS vs single-tenant vs customer VPC / BYOC vs on-prem / air-gapped<br>• Private endpoints, egress control, data-exfiltration perimeters<br>• IAM and secrets in the customer's cloud |

### D11 · Observability, Reliability & Cost — 7%

*Why this weight:* A full JD bullet (traces, token use, latency, cost) plus "troubleshooting across layers"; Richard Xu ch13-14. Runaway cost and flaky behaviour in production are classic FDE scenario questions.

*Sources:* Richard Xu ch13, ch14; goday ch8, ch10; external: [otel-genai](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/)

| ID | Tag | Subtopic | Share | Eff. | MCQs | Key concepts |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| D11.1 | `obs.tracing` | Tracing and telemetry for AI systems | 30% | 2.1% | 4 | • Traces and spans across model and tool calls; structured logs; metrics<br>• OpenTelemetry and its GenAI semantic conventions; correlation IDs<br>• Replaying a run; logging prompts and outputs without leaking PII |
| D11.2 | `obs.troubleshooting` | Troubleshooting across layers | 25% | 1.8% | 4 | • Isolate the layer — network, auth, data, retrieval, prompt, model, tool<br>• Why prod differs from staging (data, permissions, config, model version)<br>• Reproducing non-deterministic failures; classifying failures |
| D11.3 | `obs.cost` | Cost control | 25% | 1.8% | 4 | • Token accounting and cost attribution per run, tenant and feature<br>• Prompt caching, routing / cascades, batching, output-length control<br>• Budgets and spend circuit breakers |
| D11.4 | `obs.slo` | SLOs and incident response | 20% | 1.4% | 3 | • Separate SLOs for availability, latency and quality; error budgets<br>• Alerting, on-call, runbooks, post-incident review |

## Cross-cutting competencies

These are assessed mainly through question *formats*, not MCQ counts. They are where CandiTech's embedded-AI sections, SQL and code questions, and AI-graded open answers come in.

| ID | Competency | Assessed via | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `x.ai-assisted` | AI-assisted execution | ai_assisted, code_project | Drive an AI assistant to a correct result: structured prompts, purposeful iteration, verifying output, catching hallucinations, knowing when to override it. CandiTech records these transcripts for review. |
| `x.decomposition` | Structured decomposition | open_text, spoken, ai_assisted | Break a vague customer problem into parts and a plan (Palantir-style decomposition round). |
| `x.python` | Hands-on Python | code, code_project |  |
| `x.sql` | Hands-on SQL | sql |  |
| `x.estimation` | Quantitative estimation | value, mcq_single | Token, cost, latency, throughput and capacity arithmetic. |
| `x.written-comms` | Written and verbal communication | open_text, spoken | Bottom line first, audience-appropriate, trade-offs explicit. |

## Question formats (mapped to CandiTech)

| Format | CandiTech equivalent | Grading | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mcq_single` | Multiple Choice | auto |  |
| `mcq_multi` | Multiple Choice (Multiple Select) | auto |  |
| `value` | Value | auto | Numeric/text answer, e.g. back-of-envelope token cost or latency. |
| `open_text` | Open Text | ai_rubric | Graded by Gemini against a rubric (CandiTech uses rubric-based AI agents on Enterprise plans). |
| `spoken` | Video | ai_rubric | Timed verbal answer; emulate with audio or a timed no-edit text box. |
| `code` | Code | auto | Python function with hidden test cases. |
| `sql` | SQL | auto | Query against provided tables (SQLite); compare result sets. |
| `ai_assisted` | AI skills section (embedded ChatGPT / Claude, transcript recorded) | ai_rubric | Candidate works with an embedded assistant; the transcript and final output are both graded. |
| `code_project` | Code Project (Beta) | auto+ai_rubric | Multi-file task with an AI coding assistant. Later phase. |

Cognitive levels to tag each question with: `recall` (Know a mainstream term or fact (keep these rare)); `apply` (Use a concept in a concrete situation); `analyze` (Diagnose a scenario, find the cause, compare options); `evaluate` (Judge a trade-off and defend a choice under constraints).

## Job-description coverage check

Every non-generic item in the Gorilla Logic JD maps to at least one subtopic. `tools/taxonomy.py --check` fails if one doesn't. Generic soft skills, seniority, and language or frontend-framework choices are left out on purpose.

| JD item | Covered by |
|---|---|
| **jd.platform-code**: Production services, APIs, SDKs, internal tools, reusable platform capabilities | D1.3, D9.1, D9.4 |
| **jd.hybrid-systems**: Agents + tools + deterministic workflows + APIs + events + human approval steps | D6.1, D6.2, D6.5, D8.3, D9.2 |
| **jd.execution**: Agent runtimes, model invocation, reusable skills, automated actions | D4.1, D4.3, D6.3 |
| **jd.orchestration**: Routing, sequencing, parallelism, delegation, retries, checkpoints, scheduling, memory, state | D6.2, D6.4, D6.5, D9.3 |
| **jd.enterprise-context**: MCP, RAG, repos, tickets, docs, DBs, search, APIs | D5.1, D5.2, D5.3, D6.3 |
| **jd.integrations**: GitHub, Azure DevOps, Jira, Slack, cloud, SaaS | D9.4 |
| **jd.governance**: Identity, permissions, policies, approval gates, guardrails, access control, audit trails, kill switches | D4.5, D5.2, D8.1, D8.2, D8.3, D8.4, D10.3 |

## Terminology policy

Questions test principles and mainstream vocabulary. Labels coined by either handbook are never the thing being tested. Full register: [`data/terminology.yaml`](../data/terminology.yaml).

| Term | Source | Status | Policy | Mainstream reading |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dev vs. Delta | goday ch1, ch11 | divergent | concept-only | Palantir's "Dev versus Delta" names two engineering roles — Devs build the platform (one capability, many customers); Deltas (forward deployed software engineers) deploy it (one customer, many capabilities). |
| Minimum Viable Value (MVV) | goday ch2 | book-coined | concept-only | MVP / pilot scoped to a measurable business outcome; success metrics agreed up front; time to value. |
| Two-loop evaluation lifecycle (inner / outer loop) | goday ch9 | book-coined | concept-only | Offline evaluation (pre-release, golden / regression sets) vs online evaluation (production sampling and monitoring). |
| Answer Relevance = cosine(answer, query) | goday ch9 | divergent | concept-only | In RAGAS, answer relevancy generates questions from the answer with an LLM and averages their embedding similarity to the original question; it is not a direct answer-to-query cosine. |
| AutoSxS | goday ch9 | vendor | concept-only | Pairwise (side-by-side) LLM-as-judge comparison producing a win rate. |
| VPC Service Controls, Shared VPC, Access Context Manager, Private Service Connect | goday ch5, ch6 | vendor | concept-only | Data-exfiltration perimeters, centrally managed networks, context-aware access, private endpoints. |
| Workload Identity (Federation) | goday ch5 | mainstream | test | Exists across clouds (GCP, AWS IRSA / Pod Identity, Azure Workload Identity). Principle — no long-lived keys. |
| LlamaParse, LangGraph, ADK | goday ch7, ch8, ch11 | vendor | concept-only | Document parsing; stateful graph orchestration; agent frameworks. |
| MECE, Pyramid Principle | goday ch2 | mainstream | test |  |
| Medallion architecture (bronze / silver / gold) | goday ch4 | mainstream | concept-only | Databricks-originated name for layered raw / cleaned / curated pipelines; low weight for FDE. |
| Salting (data skew), dbt tests, star schema, OBT | goday ch4 | mainstream | concept-only | Data-engineering depth beyond most FDE exams; only D5.5 at light weight. |
| Reciprocal Rank Fusion, BM25, hybrid search, cross-encoder reranker | goday ch7 | mainstream | test |  |
| A2A (Agent-to-Agent protocol) | goday ch11 | mainstream | test | Awareness level only. |
| Echo / Delta | richardxu ch1 | mainstream | test | Palantir terms — Echo (deployment strategist) and Delta (forward deployed software engineer). |
| The Four Responsibilities (discovery / production / adoption / feedback) | richardxu ch1 | book-coined | concept-only | FDE spans discovery, building to production, adoption, and feeding learnings back to product. |
| The three tests (where code goes, where experience goes, how it's priced) | richardxu ch2 | book-coined | concept-only |  |
| The five filters; the discovery deliverables | richardxu ch6 | book-coined | concept-only | Problem prioritisation (value, feasibility, data, risk, sponsorship); discovery outputs. |
| Minimum Viable Deployment (MVD); the three "real" conditions | richardxu ch7 | book-coined | concept-only | Pilot / MVP with real users, real data and a real workflow; not a demo. |
| Outcome acceptance sheet; operational readiness checklist; responsibility handoff table | richardxu ch8 | book-coined | concept-only | Acceptance criteria; production / operational readiness review; RACI / ownership of failure modes. |
| The eight walls (PoC to production) | richardxu ch9 | book-coined | concept-only | The PoC-to-production gap ("pilot purgatory") — data access, integration, permissions, reliability, evaluation, cost, ownership. |
| Harness | richardxu ch9 | mainstream | test | Increasingly standard ("agent harness"); the Gorilla Logic JD uses "AI Harness". |
| Data contract | richardxu ch10 | divergent | concept-only | In data engineering a data contract is a schema / quality / SLA agreement between data producers and consumers. Richard Xu uses it for an access agreement (scope, visibility, retention, audit) — test that as data access agreement / DPA. |
| Tool contract / ToolSpec; run state machine; approval ticket | richardxu ch9, ch11 | book-coined | concept-only | Tool schemas with parameter validation; durable execution / checkpointing; human-in-the-loop approval step. |

| Four resilience primitives (timeout, retry, idempotency, graceful degradation) | richardxu ch13-14 | book-coined | concept-only | The grouping is the book's; each item is mainstream and testable by name. |
| Model routing; budget circuit breaker; cost attribution; SLO | richardxu ch14 | mainstream | test |  |
| Activation (vs go-live) | richardxu ch15 | mainstream | test | Standard product-analytics term. |

| China-specific FDE model; "who defines the last mile"; the trio; Tu FDE | richardxu ch18, ch26, ch27 | book-coined | do-not-test |  |
